newsitem.title: UK: Britain says Burma needs path back to democracy.
newsitem.headline: Britain says Burma needs path back to democracy.

text.p: Britain told Burma's ambassador to London on Tuesday that his country's military government had to prepare for a return to democracy.

Britain has consistently criticised Burma's military rulers, the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), which refused to recognise a landslide victory for the opposition National League for Democracy (NLD) in a 1990 election.

Keeping up the pressure, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told ambassador U Win Aung during a regular meeting on Tuesday that there was fear in Burma that SLORC would remain in power, "depriving the peaceful population of their right to democracy".
"It is imperative that a programme for Burma's return to democracy be prepared," Rifkind told the ambassador according to a foreign office spokesman.
Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi on Tuesday criticised SLORC for what she termed continued repression of the opposition and vowed to press her fight for democracy.
"This is persecution of the NLD," she told a news conference in Rangoon. "The situation is getting worse all the time."

Suu Kyi, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for her non-violent efforts towards democracy, was placed under virtual house arrest in December for what it said was her own safety after student street demonstrations.
Suu Kyi says she does not need nor want the protection.
The daughter of independence leader Aung San, Suu Kyi was under official house arrest for six years for her outspoken attacks on the military government. She was released in 1995.
